run_info.method: 250 sequential curl requests from one client IP, issued as fast as a shell loop allows (~3s wall clock, so ~6 tokens accrue during a token-bucket run)
notes: Not a throughput benchmark. This measures rate limiter BEHAVIOUR — how many requests each algorithm admits from a burst — not requests/sec.
Both algorithms allow the same sustained rate of 120 requests/min. They differ entirely in how they treat a burst.
Token bucket banks unused capacity: 200 tokens sat available, so 200 requests passed instantly, plus ~6 that refilled during the ~3.2s the burst took.
Sliding window enforces a hard ceiling over any 60s stretch: exactly 120 admitted, no burst allowance, exact to the request.
The sliding window result was reproduced after waiting 65s for the window to clear — 120/130 both times.

Memory cost differs sharply: sliding window stores one boxed Long timestamp per request in the window (120 per active IP), token bucket stores two fields. This is the argument for the sliding-window COUNTER variant at scale.

Both limiters key on the socket address. Behind a load balancer every request would appear to come from one IP and the whole internet would share a single limit — X-Forwarded-For handling is not implemented.
